item.title: Health Insurance Plans: Up to 900,000 Switchers Expected Next Year
item.description: Between 600,000 and 900,000 insured individuals could switch health insurance providers next year. This finding comes from a YouGov survey conducted for Deloitte among 1,236 people.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Between 600,000 and 900,000 insured individuals may switch health insurance providers - More than half review their health insurance coverage every year - 88% rate their knowledge as average to very good
## Key Facts Forecast → between 600,000 and 900,000 health insurance plan switches Survey → YouGov for Deloitte Period → third quarter of 2026 Sample → 1,236 people from German-speaking Switzerland, French-speaking Switzerland, and Ticino Self-assessed knowledge → 88% rate their knowledge as average to very good Increase in Ticino in 2027 → 3.7%
BERN — Between 600,000 and 900,000 insured individuals could switch health insurance providers next year. This is the forecast from a recent survey by the consulting firm Deloitte, which examined how insured individuals monitor and evaluate their health insurance.
The analysis was published on Friday. The survey was conducted by the research firm YouGov on behalf of Deloitte in the third quarter of 2026. A total of 1,236 people from German-speaking Switzerland, French-speaking Switzerland, and Ticino participated.
### The Survey and the Sample
More than half of the policyholders surveyed said they review their health insurance annually. This frequency is higher than average among young adults aged 18 to 29 and, regionally, among residents of French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino.
The text therefore distinguishes young adults from the other participants and juxtaposes this difference with the regional one. German-speaking Switzerland, French-speaking Switzerland, and Ticino are included in the same sample, but the focus on reviewing coverage is greater in French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino.
The figure of 600,000–900,000 remains the central estimate of the analysis. Deloitte does not present this as a final tally but as a projection of the number of insured individuals who might switch health insurance providers in the period following the survey.
The time frame must be kept separate: responses were collected in the third quarter of 2026, while the forecast looks ahead to next year. This distinction allows the data to be interpreted without confusing the timing of the survey with the final outcome of potential switches.
To explore the topic of health insurance in a manner consistent with this news article, you can consult the comparison of health insurance plans and use it alongside the survey results. The most significant impact on personal budgets becomes apparent in the scenario of a 20-franc-per-month premium increase. Nearly half of the participants would consider switching health insurers. A year ago, that figure was still just over one-third. This comparison indicates greater sensitivity compared to the previous survey, though this intention has not yet translated into an actual switch.
### Premiums and Financial Concerns
In the current survey, about a quarter of participants reported having difficulty paying their premiums. More than half of those surveyed said that health insurance premiums cause them financial concerns. The two responses reflect different levels: one concerns actual difficulty in paying, while the other reflects the perceived financial burden. Together, they show why a potential increase could influence the choice of insurer.
Knowledge of the system also shapes this perspective. Deloitte notes that people with limited knowledge of health insurance are particularly affected by financial concerns and payment difficulties. Eighty-eight percent of respondents rated their knowledge as average to very good, but only about half answered four knowledge questions on the topic correctly. The survey thus compares personal perception with the actual results of the responses.
The material linked to the news article includes a distinct figure: for 2027, in Ticino, the reported increase is 3.7%. This figure refers to the increase and not to the percentage of policyholders who consider the change; conflating the two pieces of information without distinguishing between them would lead to interpreting different measures as equivalent.
Artificial intelligence rounds out the picture. Today, one in eight people say they use it as an informational and decision-making tool for insurance-related questions. According to the survey, about one-quarter plan to consult it in the future for insurance matters: its role remains secondary, but the expected share is larger than the current one.
To track the impact of premiums on personal expenses, the survey can be used alongside the guide on costo della vita in Svizzera.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. To turn the survey results into a personal assessment, it’s best to follow a brief, repeatable process. The data allows you to focus on four key areas: the annual review, your response to a potential increase, your level of knowledge, and the use of AI as a support tool.
### Four Steps for Self-Assessment
1. Review your health insurance annually. This is the frequency reported by more than half of the respondents and provides a practical benchmark to ensure you don’t put off evaluating your situation.
2. Assess how you would react to a premium increase. The survey uses a potential increase of 20 francs per month as a benchmark: asking yourself whether you would consider switching insurers in this situation helps clarify your decision-making threshold.
3. Distinguish between personal confidence and actual knowledge. 88% rate their knowledge as average to very good, while only about half answered four questions on the topic correctly. This finding suggests that one should not rely solely on self-assessment.
4. Consider the AI as a source of information and a decision-making tool. One in eight people already uses it for insurance-related questions, and about a quarter plan to consult it. According to the survey, its role remains secondary for now.
This sequence does not equate to an automatic decision to switch: the survey measures stated intentions and behaviors, not a choice that has already been made. Rather, it serves to organize the review process, distinguishing between the cost of the premium, knowledge of the system, and the tools used to gather information.

item.description: Deloitte estimates that 600,000 to 900,000 people will switch health insurance providers; by 2027, the average premium will rise by 5% to 412 francs per month.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Deloitte estimates 600,000–900,000 cash payments - In 2027, the average premium will rise by 5% to 412 francs - One-quarter report difficulty paying premiums - With an additional 20 francs, one in two is considering switching providers
## Key Facts - Deloitte estimate → 600,000–900,000 policy switches - Survey → 1,236 participants - Research firm → YouGov - Period → third quarter of the year - 2027 increase → 5% - Average premium → 412 francs per month - Average increase → 19.70 francs per month - Inflation threshold → 20 francs per month per person
Deloitte estimates that between 600,000 and 900,000 insured individuals will switch health insurance providers. The consulting firm bases this forecast on the results of a survey and links the figure to recurring premium increases, which have made the public cost-conscious.
The survey was conducted by YouGov in the third quarter of the year and involved 1,236 participants from across Switzerland. The survey’s sample is therefore nationwide, while the results highlight certain patterns of behavior that are more common among specific age groups and regions.
### An Annual Review
More than half of those surveyed say they review their health insurance every year. Young adults aged 18 to 29 do so more often than average. Residents of Ticino and French-speaking Switzerland also report this above-average frequency.
The annual review and switching health insurance plans are two distinct processes. The survey examines, on the one hand, the habit of reviewing one’s health insurance and, on the other, the willingness to consider switching when premiums increase. Deloitte interprets both trends as a reflection of the cost sensitivity driven by recurring inflation. To track the comparison between insurers and the issue of cassa malati, the key figure to keep in mind is the frequency with which policyholders revisit their insurance coverage.
### The Threshold Indicated by the Survey
When price increases reach 20 francs per month per person, one in two policyholders considers switching insurers. A year ago, that proportion was still just over one-third. The comparison thus indicates a greater willingness to consider another insurer, but it does not mean that every consideration leads to an actual switch.
A quarter of participants also report having difficulty paying their premiums. Last Tuesday, a 5% increase in the average premium was announced for 2027, bringing it to 412 francs per month. The average increase will be 19.70 francs per month. These are the figures underlying Deloitte’s estimate: the pressure is evident in the annual insurance review, in the inflation threshold that triggers a comparison, and in the payment difficulties reported by respondents. The figure of 412 francs should be understood as a monthly average for 2027. It is not presented as the individual amount for each insured person. The same caution applies to the 19.70 francs, which is indicated as the average monthly increase. To understand the impact on your personal budget, you must base your comparison on the premium you actually pay and the change applied to you individually.
### From National Data to Personal Expenses
In the Swiss system, the LAMal/KVG premium is a per-capita expense: it is not a tax and it is not a payroll deduction. Premiums vary by canton and region, while premium reductions are determined at the cantonal level. This distinction is important for interpreting the news without treating the national figure as a one-size-fits-all number.
The Deloitte survey captures the reaction to costs; it does not replace an assessment of individual circumstances. The 20-franc threshold is monthly and per person; the average premium of 412 francs, on the other hand, is expressed on a monthly basis and represents an average. The 5% and 19.70 francs also describe the average increase announced for 2027. These are different indicators and should be kept separate when assessing the impact on costo della vita in Svizzera.
| Indicator | Practical Interpretation | |---|---| | Average Premium 2027 | 412 francs per month, announced average value | | Average Increase | 5%, equal to an additional 19.70 francs per month | | Threshold observed by Deloitte | 20 francs per month per person | | Response to the threshold | One in two policyholders is considering switching | | Reported difficulties | One-quarter of respondents struggle to pay premiums |
### Why the comparison matters
The estimate of between 600,000 and 900,000 switches does not represent an actual count: it is a Deloitte forecast based on the survey results. Similarly, the fact that a policyholder is considering a switch does not mean they will actually make one. The difference between intention and decision makes it necessary to look at one’s own premium amount, not just the national average.
The result is particularly clear for those who already check their insurance coverage frequently. Deloitte notes an above-average frequency among 18- to 29-year-olds and among residents of Ticino and French-speaking Switzerland. For these groups, regular review is the practical step that allows them to gauge any increase before deciding whether to stay with their current provider or switch. The difficulty in paying premiums reported by a quarter of respondents adds a second criterion: the premium must also be evaluated in terms of the affordability of the monthly expense.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare CHF-EUR exchange options and banks for cross-border workers. The transition from a general overview to a personal decision can be organized as an annual review, without confusing national estimates with individual amounts.
### Four Steps for the Review
1. Review your health insurance every year. This is the approach reported by more than half of those surveyed, and it ensures you don’t face a rate increase without first assessing your situation.
2. Note your actual monthly premium and distinguish it from the national average. The 412 francs announced for 2027 is an average; the 19.70 francs is the average increase. For your own assessment, the figure that matters is the one applicable to you personally.
3. Calculate the monthly increase per person. The threshold indicated by Deloitte is 20 francs: once this is reached, one in two policyholders considers switching insurers. This figure guides the assessment but does not replace the individual’s decision.
4. Assess the affordability of the premium. One-quarter of participants report difficulty paying; therefore, the comparison must include the practical ability to cover the monthly expense, not just interest in another insurer.
### From Review to Choice
The frequency of the review can be tailored to the profile indicated by the survey. Young adults between the ages of 18 and 29, as well as residents of Ticino and French-speaking Switzerland, review their insurance more often than average. For those in these groups, regular review is already the behavior observed in the survey; for others, the survey still indicates that annual review is the practice of the majority.
The most prudent approach is to distinguish between three elements: the announced average premium, the increase applicable to one’s own situation, and the actual difficulty in paying. Only after this review can one decide whether to consider switching health insurance plans, as the policyholders described by Deloitte do. ## At a Glance - The fall session of the Federal Chambers ends today - Only final votes are scheduled in the Council of States - There are 17 items on the Council of States’ agenda - The winter session will run from November 30 to December 18
## Key Facts - Location: Bern - Closing date: today - Council of States: final votes only - Items on the Council of States’ agenda: 17 - Winter session: November 30 through December 18
In Bern, the fall session of the Federal Chambers concludes today, but the final day’s agenda differs between the two chambers. In the National Council, the plenary session will address several motions and parliamentary initiatives before the traditional final votes. It will then move on to petitions and non-controversial parliamentary statements.
The sequence is therefore structured. The National Council is not merely called upon to vote on final resolutions: the agenda first includes the aforementioned parliamentary acts, followed by the session’s closing phase. The agenda thus strings together different parts of the same day, from the discussion of motions and initiatives to the subsequent phase covering petitions and non-controversial parliamentary statements.
### Two Agendas for the Final Day
In the Council of States, the agenda is more focused. Only final votes are scheduled, covering 17 items that have completed the parliamentary process. The key number for the day is therefore 17: these items are in the final stage of the parliamentary process.
The difference between the two agendas provides a clear picture of the closing of the fall session. For the National Council, the day includes even more steps before the final vote. For the Council of States, the agenda is already limited to the final vote on the 17 items that have reached the end of the parliamentary process.
The calendar is already looking ahead to the next session. The winter session will be held from November 30 to December 18. November 30 marks the start of the next session, while December 18 indicates its scheduled conclusion. These dates serve as the reference points for the transition from the fall session to the winter session.
For those following the work of the Federal Chambers, this news thus establishes three key points: today’s conclusion of the fall session, the final vote on the 17 items on the Council of States’ agenda, and the timeframe from November 30 to December 18. The National Council’s schedule remains separate, as the additional debates listed are scheduled to take place before the final votes. For the reader, the practical implication of this is, above all, the ability to distinguish the various stages of the parliamentary process, without attributing any consequences to the 17 items beyond those associated with their respective stages. For items before the Council of States, the source links the final votes to the fact that they have completed the parliamentary process. The correct interpretation, therefore, is limited to the verifiable facts: 17 items in the Council of States and a still-pending agenda in the National Council.
### The Difference Between the Two Chambers

item.title: Deloitte forecasts up to 900,000 health insurance plan switches
item.description: Deloitte forecasts between 600,000 and 900,000 health insurance plan switches. Nearly half would consider switching for an additional 20 francs per month.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Deloitte forecasts 600,000–900,000 health insurance switches - More than half review their insurance coverage every year - Nearly half would consider switching if it cost 20 francs more per month - About a quarter struggle to pay their premiums
## Key Facts - Company → Deloitte - Survey → YouGov, third quarter of 2026 - Participants → 1,236 people - Regions → German-speaking Switzerland, French-speaking Switzerland, and Ticino - Considered increase → 20 francs per month - Expected switch → between 600,000 and 900,000 policyholders - Self-reported knowledge → 88% rated as average to excellent - AI usage → 1 in 8 people; about a quarter intend to use it
Between 600,000 and 900,000 insured individuals could switch health insurance providers. This is Deloitte’s projection, which links the potential shift to annual premium increases and a population that has become more price-sensitive.
The data comes from the presentation of the results of a recent survey. More than half of the insured individuals surveyed said they review their health insurance every year. This behavior is not evenly distributed: young people between the ages of 18 and 29 and residents of French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino check their premiums more often than average. For those seeking a practical benchmark, confronto della cassa malati thus falls right in the middle of the survey results.
### The 20-franc threshold
Nearly half of the participants would consider switching insurers if their premium increased by 20 francs per month. This proportion has risen compared to a year ago, when it was just over one-third. The difference between the two surveys indicates greater responsiveness to an increase expressed as a specific monthly figure, though this does not necessarily translate into an actual switch.
The survey was conducted by Yougov on behalf of Deloitte in the third quarter of 2026. A total of 1,236 people from German-speaking Switzerland, French-speaking Switzerland, and Ticino participated.
The responses also reveal people’s ability to cover these costs. In the latest survey, about a quarter of participants reported having difficulty paying their premiums, while for more than half of those surveyed, health insurance premiums are a source of financial concern. Deloitte adds that people with little knowledge of the subject are the ones most affected by both of these challenges.
The findings on knowledge reveal a second point of contrast. Eighty-eight percent of respondents rate their knowledge of the health insurance system as average to excellent, but only slightly less than half answered four questions on the subject correctly. Artificial intelligence, on the other hand, remains a secondary tool: one in eight people use it as an information and decision-making aid, while about a quarter intend to do so. Deloitte therefore anticipates a possible increase in its use, starting from a level that is still modest. To interpret the data at the national level, it is necessary to distinguish between three factors: the intention to switch, difficulty making payments, and the frequency with which people check their premiums. The survey presents these as distinct indicators. Comparing one’s insurance plan each year does not mean one has already decided to switch; similarly, expressing financial concerns does not mean that a switch to another insurer has already taken place.
### What the Numbers Actually Measure
The framework is the LAMal/KVG: health insurance is mandatory for residents; premiums are per capita and vary by canton and region. This framework helps interpret the data for French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino: Deloitte reports an above-average frequency of comparison in these areas. The result therefore reflects a tendency to compare options, not a ranking of premiums.
A comparison of the two surveys highlights the shift in price sensitivity:
| Indicator | One year ago | Latest survey | | Participants who would consider switching for an extra 20 francs per month | Just over one-third | Nearly half |
The shift from just over one-third to nearly half—in the same scenario of a 20-franc monthly premium—does not equate to the number of switches that have already taken place. It does, however, indicate that an explicit monthly change can quickly influence the policyholder’s decision. For those following the costo della vita in Svizzera, the premium becomes an item to monitor carefully, without confusing stated intent with a definitive outcome.
The second signal concerns financial sustainability. About a quarter of participants report difficulty paying, and more than half associate premiums with financial concerns. The data suggests two interpretations: comparison shopping can help in finding a more affordable price, while difficulty in understanding the system can make the choice less straightforward. It is therefore not enough to simply ask whether the policyholder understands the system: 88% rate their understanding as average to excellent, but less than half correctly answer all four questions.
AI should also be viewed as an indicator of future behavior. Today, one in eight people uses it, and about a quarter intend to do so: this percentage may grow, but the survey does not present AI as a substitute for decision-making. For the user, the practical point is to verify the information before turning it into a decision.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. The most practical way to use these findings is to make this comparison an annual event. There’s no need to assume that changing is always the right choice: the survey reflects greater price sensitivity, not a one-size-fits-all recommendation.
### Five things to check before making a choice
- Review your health insurance once a year. This is the frequency reported by more than half of the respondents; residents of French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino, as well as young people between the ages of 18 and 29, compare plans more frequently than average. - Compare your current premium with available alternatives. Use a monthly increase of 20 francs as a benchmark—a change that nearly half of the participants would consider. - If the cost is a problem, check whether you’re eligible for a cantonal premium reduction. The survey finds that about a quarter report payment difficulties; premium reductions are administered at the cantonal level. - Assess your understanding before making a decision. 88% rate their knowledge as average to excellent, but just under half answered four questions correctly: self-assessment alone is not enough. - Use AI as an information and decision-making tool, not as an automatic process. Currently, one in eight people uses it, while about a quarter of respondents intend to do so; before making a choice, verify the information you’ve obtained.
This process helps distinguish three steps: reviewing the premium, assessing the impact of an increase, and verifying that you understand the system. For those living in Ticino or French-speaking Switzerland, the above-average frequency of comparison indicated by Deloitte offers a concrete benchmark for scheduling an annual review; for young people between the ages of 18 and 29, the guidance is similar.
The survey measures habits and stated intentions. Individual decision-making therefore requires applying general data to one’s own situation, without interpreting Deloitte’s estimate as an automatic invitation to switch insurers. To move from checking premiums to comparing options, use comparatore LAMal e cassa malati.

item.title: Average Salaries by Occupation in Switzerland in 2026: Canton of Geneva
item.description: 2026 Comparison of Professions and Cantons: In Geneva, gross income should be calculated after deducting 5.3% for AVS/AI/IPG, taxes, LAMal, and LPP.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - No federal minimum wage; some cantons have their own. - The median wage is indexed annually. - Geneva’s costs must be considered in light of taxes, insurance premiums, and the cost of living. - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% paid by the employee.
## Key Facts - Median wage → indexed annually - Taxes → IFD + cantonal + municipal - AVS/AI/IPG → 5.3% employee contribution - LAMal/KVG → mandatory for residents - Maximum workweek → 45 or 50 hours - Maternity leave → 14 weeks at 80% pay
## The 2026 comparison is based on gross pay In 2026, the comparison of average wages by profession in Switzerland cannot be reduced to a single figure. The canton of Geneva serves as the reference point for canton-level analysis, while a national comparison requires breaking down data by profession, sector, and region. The median wage is among the figures indexed annually: the data should therefore be interpreted in the context of its specific reference year and an official source, without treating any amount as fixed beyond its indexation.
### Distinguishing Between Responsibilities Statistics and taxation fall under different jurisdictions. The FSO/BFS collects and produces statistics but does not set tax rates. The tax system is organized into three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax, and municipal tax. Each canton has its own law and multiplier; the municipality applies a multiplier to the cantonal rate. AFC/ESTV oversees direct federal tax and VAT, while cantonal administrations manage the cantonal and municipal levels. UFAS/BSV handles social security—AVS/AHV, AI, and LPP—and does not set tax rates.
### What’s Included in Your Paycheck Gross pay is not the same as net pay. AVS/AI/IPG contributions amount to 5.3% for the employee and 10.6% in total when combined with the employer’s share. AD/AC is 1.1% up to the annual cap. LAINF/LAA ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector. For the LPP/BVG, the rates applied to the coordinated salary are 7% for those aged 25 to 34, 10% for those aged 35 to 44, 15% for those aged 45 to 54, and 18% from age 55 up to the reference age.
For this reason, a table showing the average salary by profession must be supplemented by a review of the pay stub: the gross amount alone does not indicate what remains after contributions and taxes. To examine the individual line items in more detail, consult the busta paga svizzera, keeping salary, social security, and taxes separate. ## Geneva as a Point of Comparison, Not a Ranking To analyze the canton of Geneva on a national scale, the question is not simply which profession has the highest salary. One must consider the sector, cantonal regulations, the municipality, and non-salary-related expenses all within the same framework. An average or median cannot replace an examination of the specific job offer and the statistical year.
### Three filters for a proper comparison The first filter is tax-related. Two job offers with the same gross salary can yield different results depending on the canton or municipality, because the tax system includes direct federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes, and the municipality applies its own multiplier to the cantonal rate. Therefore, it is not enough to compare only the federal tax rate; cantonal and municipal data must be considered separately.
The second filter is the cost of living. For residents, LAMal/KVG coverage is mandatory and must be obtained within three months of arrival. The premium is per person, varies by canton or region, and is neither a tax nor an employer contribution; there is also a premium reduction available through cantonal subsidies. Deductibles for adults are CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, or 2,500. To get the full picture, the salary should be cross-referenced with costo della vita in Svizzera and the LAMal e cassa malati guide.
The third filter concerns the job offer. The maximum workweek is 45 hours in manufacturing, office work, and sales, or 50 hours in other sectors. The minimum vacation time is four weeks, or five weeks for those under 20 years of age. Maternity and paternity leave affect the overall value of the job: maternity leave lasts 14 weeks at 80% of pay through IPG, while paternity leave lasts two weeks. A comparison by profession that ignores these conditions remains incomplete.
The minimum wage must also be addressed accurately: there is no single federal threshold, while some cantons have their own. When moving to Geneva or another canton, those arriving from abroad must distinguish between an L permit (valid for up to one year), a renewable B permit, a C residence permit, and a G permit for cross-border workers. For the C permit, the standard requirement is typically 10 years of residence, reduced to 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens. The permit is not a salary, but it is part of the practical considerations to evaluate before relocating.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the pension planner and the pillar 3 simulator. ## How to Evaluate a Job Offer in 2026 The most reliable way to compare a professional salary in Geneva with that of another canton is to compile the data into a comparison sheet. Generic rankings aren’t helpful—you need the statistical year, profession, industry, work location, and salary components.
1. Establish the baseline data. Use a FSO statistic for 2026 or the year specified by the source, and note whether it refers to the mean or the median. The median salary is one of the figures indexed annually: do not substitute a value from another year without indicating so.
2. Break down the taxes. Specify the canton and municipality, then consider the three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax, and municipal tax. For tax reporting and calculation, you can refer to dichiarazione delle imposte. AFC/ESTV is the reference for direct federal income tax (IFD) and VAT; cantonal administrations are the point of contact for the cantonal and municipal components.
3. Recalculate the taxable net income. Enter AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% for the employee, AD/AC at 1.1% up to the annual cap, LAINF/LAA between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector, and LPP/BVG on the coordinated salary: 7% for ages 25–34, 10% for ages 35–44, 15% for ages 45–54, and 18% from age 55 up to the reference age. Do not confuse these items with the LAMal/KVG premium.
4. Check your health insurance coverage. If you are a resident, health insurance is mandatory and must be obtained within three months of arrival. Compare the premium tier, the adult deductible you choose (CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, or 2,500), and any cantonal discount; the premium is per person and is not deducted from your salary.
5. Read the contract carefully, not just the numbers. Check the maximum work hours, vacation time, leave, and cancellation terms: 45 or 50 hours per week depending on the sector, at least four weeks of vacation, 14 weeks of maternity leave at 80% pay, two weeks of paternity leave, and notice periods of 1, 2, or 3 months—in the first year, from the second to the ninth year, and from the tenth year onward, respectively. If you are a foreign national, also verify the permit category indicated by the SEM (L, B, C, or G).
### The Final Check Before comparing two offers, keep salary, taxes, social security, and insurance separate. UFAS/BSV handles AVS/AI/LPP and not taxes; UST/BFS handles statistics and not tax rates. This separation prevents you from adding an item of a different nature to the gross amount or from attributing the wrong area of responsibility to an authority.
After gathering these elements, you can estimate your individual result using the calcolatore stipendio.

The median salary is an indexed figure every year: the updated comparison must therefore start from the official figure for the year, without transforming a general value into a figure valid for each profession or region.
### The gross is not enough
The first step is to separate the gross salary from the available money. The Swiss tax system has three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax. Each canton applies its own law and multiplier; the municipality applies the multiplier on the cantonal tax. The gross salary itself, therefore, must be interpreted considering the place of taxation.

FSIO/BSV concerns social security, including AHV/AHV, IV and BVG/BVG, but does not set taxes. FSO/BFS produces statistics and does not set rates. Separate contributions are then made to the salary. AHV/IV/EO weighs 5.3% on the employee and 10.6% overall with the employer. AD/AC is equal to 1.1% up to the annual ceiling. The UVG/LAA varies from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector. For the BVG on the coordinated salary, the indicated brackets are 7% between 25 and 34 years old, 10% between 35 and 44, 15% between 45 and 54 and 18% from the age of 55 up to the reference age.

In a hypothetical scenario, two employees with the same gross may have a different result if they change canton, municipality, sector or housing situation. The reason for this is not just one rate: it is the sum of taxes, insurance and employment rules.
### Four variables to compare
| Factor | Verified Rule | How the Reading Changes | |---|---|---| | Canton and commune | Each canton has its own law and multiplier; the commune applies the multiplier to the canton | The net tax is not read from the national gross | | Minimum wage | There is no federal minimum; some cantons have their own | An offer must also be checked against the cantonal rule | | Residence and health | KVG is compulsory for residents, with premiums per canton or region and cantonal premium reductions | The premium is per capita, not a tax or wage contribution | | Industry and contract | Maximum working hours of 45 hours in industry, offices and sales, 50 hours in other sectors | Working time completes the economic comparison |
The KVG must be kept separate from the paycheck: compulsory health insurance is private and is paid for with a per capita premium. Those who arrive in Switzerland must take it out within 3 months of arrival. The premium depends on the canton and region, while the premium reduction is cantonal. For this reason, when calculating the cost of living, it is more correct to add the health item to the budget instead of treating it as a deduction from salary. The costo della vita in Svizzera helps to keep these plans separate.
The contract also changes the concrete value of the offer. The minimum holiday is four weeks, which becomes five under the age of 20. Maternity lasts 14 weeks at 80% through EO and paternity leave two weeks. The notice periods are one month in the first year, two from the second to the ninth and three from the tenth.
The house adds another check. The Federal Tenancy Act, CO Art. 253 et seq., applies in the same way in every canton: the security deposit does not exceed three months' rent and goes to an escrow account in the name of the tenant. A landlord's notice of termination is only valid on the official cantonal form and can be challenged within 30 days to the conciliation authority. FSIO/BSV and FSO/BFS remain different references, respectively for social security and statistics.

For those arriving from abroad, also classify the SEM permit: L up to one year, B renewable, C usually after 10 years of residence or 5 for EU/EFTA, G for cross-border commuters. 5. Charge for the house. Before signing a tenancy, check the deposit, escrow account and official cantonal form for any landlord termination. item.description: Three arrests, eight searches and five servers seized: the operation against KillSec recovered at least 110 terabytes of stolen data.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Three arrests and eight searches in four countries - Recovered at least 110 terabytes of stolen data - Attacks on Swiss companies between October 2023 and June 2025
## Key Facts - Group → KillSec (or KillSecurity) - Operation → dismantling of an IT structure - Arrests → three - Searches → eight - Countries → Spain, Greece, the United Kingdom and Romania - Servers seized → five - Data recovered → at least 110 terabytes - → attacks against several Swiss companies, between October 2023 and June 2025
On Wednesday, a large international operation made it possible to dismantle the IT structure used by the KillSec ransomware group, also known as KillSecurity. The toll includes three arrests, eight searches in Spain, Greece, the United Kingdom and Romania, the seizure of five servers and the recovery of at least 110 terabytes of stolen data.
### The Swiss survey
This was announced by the Federal Office of Police (fedpol) and the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland (OAG). Since the summer of 2025, the two agencies have been conducting an investigation into a series of attacks against various Swiss companies, which took place between October 2023 and June 2025. The criminal proceedings concern data theft, abusive access to a computer system, data damage and extortion.
### How ransomware works
The mechanism described in the source follows a precise sequence. The perpetrators improperly enter the victim's computer system, copy and extract the data of interest, then encrypt the servers. Only then do they demand a ransom in exchange for the decryption key; the request is often made in cryptocurrency.
### Double extortion
KillSec practices the so-called double extortion. After the encryption of the servers, if the company refuses to pay, the authors threaten to publish the data on the darknet. The refusal may depend, for example, on a backup made before the theft: the restoration of the data does not eliminate, according to the dynamics described, the threat of dissemination of the information already copied.
Fedpol and the OAG participated in the investigations coordinated by Europol and Eurojust together with seven other countries. The communication released on Thursday underlines the need for cooperation between national and international partners: "Given the international nature of cybercrime, close cooperation between the different partners, both nationally and internationally, is essential," reads a statement released on Thursday. ## The risk does not end with encryption
For a Swiss company, the sequence described separates two problems. Server encryption is about access to systems; copying and extraction happen first and feed the threat of publication. The backup cited by the source can therefore explain the ransom refusal, but it does not automatically delete the second lever used by the group. It is the difference between recovering one's own systems and preventing the data already stolen from being disseminated.
| Step | What the source indicates | Pressure on the victim | |---|---|---| | Access | Unauthorized entry into the computer system | The attack starts | | Extraction | Copying data of interest | Data is stolen | | Encryption | Encrypted servers | Decryption key is asked | | Backup | Can Motivate Ransom Rejection | Darknet Threat Remains | | Payment | Ransom is often demanded in cryptocurrency | The demand takes an economic form |
### A balance sheet to be read without overinterpretation
The reference to at least 110 terabytes refers to the material recovered in the operation. The source does not attribute that volume to a single Swiss company, does not indicate the identity of the companies involved and does not report any payments. Sticking to this data avoids turning the balance sheet of the operation into an estimate of the damage for each victim.
The geography should also be read without simplification. The investigation stems from attacks against Swiss companies, while the operation involved four countries and involved the seizure of servers. The participation of fedpol and the OAG, together with Europol, Eurojust and seven other countries, shows a chain of investigation spread beyond Swiss territory alone.
The text does not indicate the sectors involved. The reference therefore remains limited to several Swiss companies; those looking for a distinct picture of the productive fabric can consult the aziende che assumono.

To examine the news correctly, those who work in a Swiss company can follow a documentary sequence without adding unconfirmed elements.
### Four checks before drawing conclusions
1. **Separate dates.** The attacks indicated in the investigation date back to the period between October 2023 and June 2025. The Swiss investigation has been conducted since the summer of 2025. The dismantling operation took place on Wednesday, while the communication was released on Thursday.
2. Distinguish the locations. The source links the attacks to different Swiss companies and indicates eight searches in Spain, Greece, the United Kingdom and Romania. The list of countries of the operation should not be transformed into a list of victims' locations.
3. Separate the numbers. Five servers are seized; at least 110 terabytes are the data recovered. The text does not assign the volume to a single company and does not quantify individual damage.
4. Use the terms of the procedure. The case concerns data theft, abusive access to a computer system, data damage and extortion. The ransom is also described as often requested in cryptocurrency, not as a payment already made.
This grid also avoids confusing a threat with an event that has already taken place. The source reports that, in the event of a refusal, KillSec threatens to publish the data on the darknet; it does not report that the data has actually been published. ## Key Facts - What: Petitions for physiotherapy fee increase - When: October 2024 (petition submission) - Who: Physioswiss (trade association) - How much: Increase required at least 30% - Signatures: 112,000 throughout Switzerland - Petitions: 26 at cantonal level - Director: Osman Bešić - New model: From 2027, billing at 5-minute intervals
The trade association Physioswiss has collected 112,000 signatures throughout Switzerland in support of higher fees for physiotherapy. Twenty-six cantonal petitions will now be submitted to the competent authorities in the course of October, the association said in a statement. Deliveries have already taken place in Neuchâtel and Zug.
### The central request: plus 30 percent Specifically, the association is calling for a fee increase of at least 30 percent. According to Physioswiss, this would allow practices to cover operating costs and pay fair salaries. A prerequisite, the statement highlights, to ensure access to physiotherapy care for all patients in the vicinity of their home. "Now the cantons are called upon to take the economic reality of physiotherapy practices seriously and to set fair rates," says director Osman Bešić, quoted in the note.
### Antecedents: the 2023-2024 conflict As early as 2023, the industry had drawn attention to its financial situation. At that time, Physioswiss had collected 283,000 signatures against a tariff intervention planned by the Federal Council, which was then implemented in spring 2024. This triggered an internal conflict that led to the creation of a new association called Prophysio. A new tariff model, which is expected to come into force in 2027, proposes a switch to performance-based pricing with a time component: physiotherapy services will be billed at five-minute intervals. The current petitions, on the other hand, concern the setting of cantonal tariff point values. ### Impact on patients and the healthcare system The requested tariff increase of 30% would have a direct impact on the KVG/KVG system. Physiotherapy services are reimbursed by compulsory health insurance on medical prescription. An adjustment of the cantonal tariffs of the tariff point would result in higher costs for health insurers, which could be reflected in the 2026 premiums. The cantons, which are responsible for setting the point values, will have to balance the sustainability of the studies with the burden on the winners.
### Comparison with the situation 2023 The current signature collection (112,000 signatures) is lower than in 2023 (283,000), when the opposition was directed against federal intervention. Today, petitions target the cantonal level, where the value of the tariff point is decided. The fragmentation into 26 separate petitions reflects the federal architecture: each canton sets its own point value, creating territorial disparities that physiotherapists have been denouncing for some time.
### The new 2027 model: opportunities and risks The transition to billing at five-minute intervals from 2027 introduces a time component that should better remunerate the complexity of treatments. Physioswiss defends this novelty. However, the transition requires management adjustments in practices and new tariff agreements between trade associations and insurers. Until 2027, the values of the cantonal point remain the main lever for economic sustainability.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ### What happens now: calendar and actors The petitions have been or will be delivered to the cantonal governments and parliaments by October 2024. Each canton will follow its own procedure: in some cases the government can decide directly, in others the approval of the legislature is required. Decision times vary from a few months to over a year. Physiotherapists and patients can monitor the process by contacting the cantonal health department or by consulting the website of the local Grand Council.
### How to orient yourself as a patient Anyone who receives physiotherapy on prescription does not pay the tariff directly: health insurance reimburses less the deductible and the deductible (10%). A tariff increase does not change the patient's share per session, but affects the overall costs of the system and thus future premiums. Checking the coverage of your health insurance company and comparing premiums remains the main tool.
